content:
Earlier this year, I swapped a petrol-powered mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. The user can manually drive the robot along the lawn boundary to create a virtual map. Once set up, the robot will mow automatically according to a preset schedule.

Recently, I tested another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I believe that for many people, this machine may be easier to use.

Camera-assisted automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each understands your lawn.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I first had to drive the mower along the boundary with my phone before it could build an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the manufacturer calls TerraVision 2.0. The mower is equipped with three cameras that can automatically map out the lawn area, eliminating the need to bury boundary wires underground or install an additional RTK antenna.

The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I think it may be simpler for people who are less familiar with computer technology.

To verify this, I asked my mother, who lives in another U.S. state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 entirely on her own, without giving her any assistance. She said everything worked fine. That said, however, I'm not entirely sure she would have had the patience to first drive the robot along the entire boundary with her phone and then mark out all the areas to avoid.

During the automatic mapping in the front yard, a few small issues came up. There is no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, so the TerraMow initially included part of the neighbour's lawn in my map.

I set that area as a no-go zone in the app, and the problem was resolved. That said, if there is no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, extra care is needed when creating the initial map.

Looking through the mower's cameras

The cameras on the TerraMow also enable one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used the iPhone's screen mirroring feature to cast that video onto my Mac's large display. I could sit indoors working while watching from the mower's perspective as it moved around the backyard.

This feature isn't essential for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more interesting, and sometimes explains why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 has no equivalent live camera view feature.

Beyond that, the two iPhone apps share many common features. Both support preset schedules, mowing mode adjustments, zoning, no-go zone markers, and remote control of the mower.

As for that last feature, the TerraMow's design is particularly thoughtful. In addition to the traditional left-and-right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-hand joystick mode. Users can hold the iPhone normally and steer the mower with their thumb.

Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically according to a preset schedule, with no human intervention. That said, the TerraMow's joystick mode is quite convenient for trimming small patches that the robot may have missed.

Sometimes I almost feel as though I'm controlling the robot by telepathy (the fun kind). I walk behind the mower holding my iPhone, give it a gentle nudge with my thumb, and it drives precisely to where I've directed it.

Every robotic mower app should copy this design.

A more aggressive mower

The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing, it cut closer to the ground while mowing, and was noticeably louder in operation.

I wouldn't say the TerraMow is "very loud," but the difference is clearly noticeable. The Anthbot runs quite quietly — even when it heads out at night with its headlights on, you can almost forget it's still running.

Because the TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. Therefore, scheduling mowing during the day becomes more important.

The V1000 feels solidly built, and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. The TerraMow package includes a protective garage that can cover the charging dock, whereas a garage for the Anthbot has to be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow has been consistently reliable. I let it mow every day for several weeks in a row, and never needed any human intervention.

When adaptive mapping gets a little too "smart"

The same visual intelligence that makes the TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts the map based on what it sees and hears. After each job, saving those changes takes a fairly long time, during which you can't perform any operations in the app.

After several days of heavy rain in a row, I ran into an interesting extreme case. Water had pooled in one spot of the yard, and the TerraMow sensibly avoided that area during its next run.

Inside the skipped circular area, the weeds grew taller and taller. After a while, the mower seemed to mistake the taller weeds there for something to avoid permanently, so that area kept being skipped even after the ground had dried out.

I used the app's remote control feature to manually drive the mower over there and cut down the taller weeds, and the problem was resolved. Once that area returned to normal, automatic mowing resumed there as well.

Regular edging also helps the TerraMow approach boundaries more confidently. Otherwise, taller grass growing along an indistinct boundary may be misidentified as an obstacle rather than part of the mowing area.

The Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on the boundaries and obstacles you set yourself. That method requires more preparation work, but it avoids the situation where the map "changes its mind" about the same patch of grass.

9to5Mac conclusion

After using both systems, for most people I lean toward recommending the TerraMow's camera-led approach.

For me, burying wires in the ground is completely out of the question, while installing an RTK base station means placing, powering, and maintaining additional hardware. The TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. Initial mapping takes longer, fuzzy boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook a weed-choked patch as a permanent obstacle.

All of these issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, a compelling live camera view, and the best manual control experience of any robotic mower app I've used.

I genuinely enjoy tending the garden, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing that chore over to a robot frees up time to look after the flower beds, do the edging, and handle detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 excels at this, and I would recommend it, especially for users who want a robotic mower but don't want to bury cables in the ground, don't want to install an RTK antenna, and don't want to walk around the entire yard holding their phone from start to finish.

Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at US$999, and a US$200 coupon code can be used on coupon sites. The product can also be purchased through the official TerraMow website.
